articles.title: Every NBA Team's Top Breakout Candidate In 2026-27
articles.summary: One of the best parts of every NBA season is seeing young players make a major leap in their overall play.
articles.body:
One of the best parts of every NBA season is seeing young players make a major leap in their overall play.

We witnessed this last year with players like Nickeil Alexander-Walker (winner of the NBA's Most Improved Player award), Ryan Rollins, Neemias Queta, Deni Avdija, and others. This could mean blossoming into an All-Star or simply a major jump in individual statistics as a rotational player in a bigger role.

The good news? All 30 teams possess at least one breakout candidate, to varying degrees. It's time to take a spin around the league and attempt to identify the one young player ready to break out.

The 23rd overall pick in 2025, Asa Newell showed flashes as a rookie yet never truly played a consistent role for an Atlanta Hawks team that was shifting identities. Now in his second year and with a clear vision in place, there should be a dedicated rotation spot for the 6'10" forward.

Newell was surprisingly efficient for a rookie, even if he wasn't getting a ton of looks on offense. The 20-year-old made 66.0 percent of his two-pointers and 38.7 percent of his three-point attempts. He attempted just 29 total free throws (making 55.2 percent) in 44 games, an area the Hawks would surely like to see improve.

The physical tools are there for a player who could be Jalen Johnson's primary backup, even as the Hawks added some rookies to the frontcourt.

One of the most overlooked aspects of the Jaylen Brown trade is its impact on Hugo González, the 28th pick in the 2025 draft.

While González certainly isn't going to replicate Brown's scoring numbers, few rookies made as big an impact on winning last season.

The 20-year-old had a swing rating of plus-9.3 last season (93rd percentile, via Cleaning the Glass ). When he was asked to play small forward, that number jumped all the way to plus-27.8 ( 100th percentile ).

Brown being gone means even more minutes for González on the wing, especially since Paul George has played more than 56 games just once in the past seven years. Don't be surprised to see González crack double digits in scoring on a nightly basis while bringing his relentless energy and defense.

Egor Dëmin showcased the most promise of any Brooklyn Nets rookie last season. There were a lot of them.

Plantar fasciitis ended his season prematurely, but Dëmin showed enough in his 52 games to earn a starting spot in the 2026-27 backcourt, even with this summer's No. 6 overall pick Mikel Brown Jr. joining the fold.

At 6'8", Dëmin can essentially play either guard position. He made 40.5 percent of his catch-and-shoot threes . That was while playing with no true point guard and sharing the backcourt with a ball-dominant Cam Thomas. Now, with Brown and Julius Randle beside him, Dëmin should get more frequent and more open looks.

Landing Spots for Top 5 Unsigned NBA Free Agents 🏀

The No. 6 overall pick in the 2024 draft, Tidjane Salaün, made some real improvements last season, largely overshadowed by the Charlotte Hornets' second-half surge and the play of rookie standout Kon Knueppel.

The 6'10" forward went from one of the NBA's worst three-point shooters as a rookie (28.3 percent) to one of its best as a sophomore (43.4 percent) despite having to take a step back in overall minutes and shot attempts.

Salaün will need to prove in training camp that he's ready for a bigger role. Last year's starting power forward Miles Bridges has since been traded, although Naz Reid, Royce O'Neale and Dorian Finney-Smith have all been added to the fold. Reid will either start or have a big role off the bench, though Salaün should be able to beat out the other veterans and carve out more minutes for himself in his third year.

Rob Dillingham has a lot to prove after the Minnesota Timberwolves essentially gave up on him in Year 2.

Traded to the Chicago Bulls before the deadline in the Ayo Dusunmu deal, Dillingham showed some growth in a consistent role off the bench. The 21-year-old averaged 9.6 points, 3.0 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 0.9 steals in 21.5 minutes, even while sharing shots and touches with players like Collin Sexton and Anfernee Simons.

Both veteran guards are now gone, with Norman Powell added in their place. This should ensure Dillingham still has a role in the rotation for a young Bulls team searching for players with upside.

Dillingham needs to become a more consistent three-point shooter playing alongside Josh Giddey and will have to battle defensively given his limited size.

The Cleveland Cavaliers' depth will be tested this season after Dean Wade and Keon Ellis left in free agency, while Dennis Schröder and Max Strus were traded to make a sign-and-trade for Peyton Watson possible.

This means a bigger opportunity for some young guys off the bench, especially Tyrese Proctor in the backcourt.

The 22-year-old former Duke standout had a solid rookie season in Cleveland, making 35.1 percent of his threes and averaging 18.0 points, 4.2 rebounds, 4.9 assists, 1.7 steals per 36 minutes of play.

Proctor spent this past summer playing for Australia in the FIBA World Cup, averaging 19.0 points and shooting 40.0 percent from three. He'll see minutes playing alongside both Donovan Mitchell and James Harden this upcoming season in what could be a breakout role.

It feels like we've known about Dereck Lively II for a long time, as the 22-year-old center was a key piece of the Dallas Mavericks' run to the 2024 NBA Finals.

Now entering his fourth year, injuries have prevented Lively from truly breaking out. Foot surgery limited him to just seven games last season, where he averaged 4.3 points and 5.3 rebounds in 16.4 minutes.

If he can make a full recovery before the start of the season (there's been no official report yet), Lively has elite rim protection potential at 7'1" and should become a favorite lob target of Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving.

The Denver Nuggets have already lost Peyton Watson, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Jonas Valančiūnas off their bench this summer. A fourth-year leap from Julian Strawther would help lighten the blow.

Strawther could be on a similar trajectory to Watson, another former late first-round pick by Denver who didn't truly shine until the final year of his rookie deal.

The 24-year-old has improved his three-point shooting year over year (to 38.7 percent last season) and averaged 14.8 points in his 14 starts. With Watson, Hardaway and possibly Bruce Brown Jr. all gone, minutes on the wing should be plentiful for the 6'6" forward who's also playing for a new contract.

The No. 5 overall pick in the 2024 NBA draft, Ron Holland II has done little to justify his draft position thus far.

No, 2024 wasn't the strongest of classes, as Holland hasn't even proven himself to be a rotation player in the playoffs. A lack of a three-point shot has overshadowed his good defensive size and instincts to this point.

If you squint hard enough, you'll see that Holland did go 10-of-19 from deep (52.6 percent) over his final five regular season games. He just turned 21 this past July, so he still has plenty of time to grow and develop.

For a Detroit Pistons team that already features two non/bad shooters, they need Holland to develop some semblance of a three-point shot to be able to play him alongside Ausar Thompson and Jalen Duren (a restricted free agent).

If his jumper looks better, we could see a breakout year from Holland.

Golden State Warriors: Brandin Podziemski, G

Brandin Podziemski has improved each of his three professional seasons, though a true breakout could come in 2026-27.

No Jimmy Butler to begin the year means more scoring opportunities for the 23-year-old guard who's eligible to sign an extension before the season begins. After Butler tore his ACL on Jan. 19, Podziemski averaged 17.8 points, 5.4 rebounds, 3.4 assists and shot 38.0 percent from three after moving into a full-time starting role.

Stephen Curry's minutes (30.9) were his lowest in 14 years (not counting his five-game 2019-2020 season) as head coach Steve Kerr loads to manage the 38-year-old's workload.

The Golden State Warriors will need Podziemski's scoring and playmaking to help keep their offense afloat while waiting for a healthy Butler to return.

Reed Sheppard already got some Most Improved Player love last season, finishing sixth in the award thanks to a much-improved sophomore campaign. Modest numbers of 13.5 points and 3.4 assists per game could easily see another big jump this season.

Yes, Fred VanVleet is back from a torn ACL and will eat into the guard minutes in this rotation. The 32-year-old is best suited in a backup role at this point in his career, especially coming off such a major injury.

Sheppard should be the starting point guard for the Houston Rockets, as the No. 3 overall pick in the 2024 draft has a ton of upside as a multifaceted scorer, ball-handler and floor-spacer when players like Kevin Durant or Amen Thompson are running the offense.

Jarace Walker saw a larger opportunity last year due to the number of injuries on the Indiana Pacers. That should set him up for a career year in 2026-27.

The 23-year-old forward saw a bump in both rebound and assist percentage in Year 3 while averaging a career-high 11.6 points per game. Walker has been a consistent outside shooter (38.6 percent) who can play either forward position.

Having a healthy Tyrese Haliburton back should help get Walker even more quality looks. Fellow forward Obi Toppin could be a trade candidate, as moving his $15 million contract could help the Pacers get out of the luxury tax .

Los Angeles Clippers: Yanic Konan Niederhäuser, C

Yanic Konan Niederhäuser is still recovering from foot surgery he suffered in March. When he returns, however, the second-year pro could be in line to be the Los Angeles Clippers' starting center.

Veteran Brook Lopez will keep the position warm for now, although the 23-year-old Niederhäuser is the Clippers' bench option for a long-term solution.

At nearly seven feet, Niederhäuser has excellent rim protection potential and averaged 11.0 points, 7.7 rebounds and 2.5 blocks while shooting 66.7 percent overall in the six games where he played 20 minutes or more.

The 30th overall pick of the 2025 draft, Niederhäuser should have a big role this season for a Clippers team that's pivoting to a younger core.

Picking a breakout candidate for the Los Angeles Lakers is difficult, as most of the talent on the roster is already in their mid-to-late 20s. Jaden Hardy, 24, still has some upside, although there's no guarantee he'll even be in the rotation.

Some reason for optimism stems from his late-season run with the Washington Wizards last season, where Hardy shot 42.0 from three while averaging 12.6 points in 20.4 minutes off the bench.

This kind of hot shooting from deep will pair nicely alongside Luka Dončić, although there would be some defensive concerns.

Memphis Grizzlies: Walter Clayton Jr., PG

The Memphis Grizzlies currently have 18 players who are 26 or younger under contract. There's no shortage of breakout options here.

The frontcourt will be a little crowded now with Cameron Boozer, Jerami Grant and Isaiah Stewart all joining the fold. However, the backcourt should come with plenty of opportunity, especially if Ty Jerome fails to stay healthy again.

Walter Clayton Jr. saw an increased role following a trade to the Grizzlies in the Jaren Jackson Jr. deal and even started six games as a rookie. The former Florida star averaged 12.3 points, 3.0 rebounds and 6.0 assists while shooting 41.9 percent from three on a healthy 31 attempts during those starts.

With Ja Morant gone, Clayton should have a big role again for Memphis, either as a starter or a key reserve.

The Miami Heat need Nikola Jović to be a big part of the team's rotation this season, especially since the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade reduced the team's overall depth.

Jović was bad last season after agreeing to a four-year, $62.4 million rookie extension that kicks in this year. Despite entering his fifth professional season, Jović just turned 23 this past summer and was battling back from various injuries in 2025-26. He looked healthier this summer, averaging 20.0 points on 76.9 percent shooting from two and 52.6 percent from three for Serbia in the FIBA Basketball World Cup 2027 European Qualifiers.

Miami doesn't have a lot of young talent to build around. Jović needs to prove he's worth this new contract and become a key rotation piece behind Antetokounmpo.

Ryan Rollins was one of the NBA's biggest surprises last season in a breakout role. Now, the Milwaukee Bucks better hope they have another candidate in Kel'el Ware.

The 22-year-old is a true 7-footer with a massive wingspan and unlimited potential. Ware needs to start either ahead of Myles Turner or alongside him.

In his 34 starts a season ago, Ware averaged a double-double with 12.8 points, 10.7 rebounds, 1.2 blocks and a 52.9/40.9/75.4 slash line. He needs to be completely unleashed on a lousy Bucks team in desperate need of star power. Ware is this franchise's next best chance at one.

Minnesota Timberwolves: Cody Williams, F

It's tempting to go with Jonathan Kuminga here, although the sixth-year forward has already topped 16 points per game in a season. Cody Williams is more of a deep cut. He should have a rotation role on a Minnesota Timberwolves team that's thin at forward.

Williams was the 10th overall pick in 2024, although a horrible rookie season with the Utah Jazz put his career in doubt. Williams was better last year, even averaging 16.4 points, 4.2 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 1.1 steals over his final 19 games.

If Williams can even become an average outside shooter, he can be an NBA rotation player and should have a career year for a Minnesota team chasing a title.

Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears are both reasonable breakout candidates here. Fears may have to wait a year for the backcourt to clear up a bit, as Jordan Poole enters the final year of his contract and Dejounte Murray has a player option for 2027-28.

Queen may have the best path to minutes, especially since Zion Williamson played in 60 games last season. Williamson has never been healthy in back-to-back seasons, averaging just 15 games in the years following a 60-plus-game season.

Queen will make the most of whatever opportunity is given. He's an extremely talented passer, good rebounder and has a strong touch around the rim. The 21-year-old averaged 13.4 points, 8.1 rebounds and 4.6 assists in his 46 starts while shooting 32.7 percent from three.

Regular season fatigue is bound to set in at some point for the defending champion New York Knicks. When it does, the franchise will need players like Mohamed Diawara to help provide a spark.

The 6'9" forward has strong defensive skills that will be called on even more while sharing the second unit with Andre Drummond instead of Mitchell Robinson. Diawara also connected on 57.6 percent of his corner three-pointers last season, proving to be a reliable kick-out option for Jalen Brunson and others.

Diawara's offensive role could slowly expand over time, although most of his impact and breakout will come on the defensive end this season.

Trading Lu Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to shed salary means more opportunity for some other guards and wings on a loaded Oklahoma City Thunder roster. The main beneficiary will be Cason Wallace, who should slide into Dort's former starting spot.

Wallace's defense has already earned recognition, as the 22-year-old was named to the All-Defense second team in his third season.

The offensive opportunities should be greater as well. Wallace was a far better three-point shooter as a starter last season (36.4 percent) than as a reserve (30.0 percent). He's not going to be a big-time scorer with so many other offensive options on this roster, although we can expect Wallace to finally put up double-digit scoring averages while he sees an uptick in overall minutes, shots and usage.

It's tempting to go with Anthony Black here, although the fourth-year guard already had a mini breakout last year (15.0 points, 3.8 rebounds, 3.7 assists). It's hard to imagine his numbers climbing much higher unless he gets traded at some point.

Jase Richardson was the 25th overall pick in the 2025 draft and may have too much offensive pop in his game to not have a bigger role in Year 2. The Orlando Magic have been desperate for efficient scoring for years. Richardson brings a combination of three-point shooting and some rim-rattling ability.

The 20-year-old guard averaged 11.0 points, 2.8 rebounds, 2.1 assists and shot 43.3 percent from three in the nine games in which he played 20 minutes or more, proving he can contribute when given the opportunity.

Averaging 16.0 points per game as a rookie was just the start for VJ Edgecombe, whose breakout may look different than most other young players'.

If Joel Embiid, LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown are all healthy, Edgecombe's raw scoring numbers will actually take a hit this season. Instead, this is a chance for the 21-year-old to improve his scoring efficiency, three-point shooting, passing and defense while becoming an all-around star.

Transition opportunities should be plentiful with James' elite look-ahead passes. The star power on this team will create plenty of wide-open looks for Edgecombe, who will need to improve his corner three-point shooting (34.5 percent).

If Embiid and James miss time due to injury or rest, Edgecombe's scoring may be needed more than we realize.

Khaman Maluach didn't make much of an impact as a rookie for the Phoenix Suns, despite being the 10th overall pick of the 2025 draft.

A strong summer league showing, combined with an injury to starter Mark Williams, could open the door to a big second year for Maluach, the former Duke star.

Williams is expected to miss several months following shoulder surgery, leaving Maluach and Oso Ighodaro in line for more minutes. Maluach looked really good at summer league, averaging 19.5 points, 12.8 rebounds, 2.0 blocks and shooting 40.0 percent from three.

If the outside shot is legit, Maluach could turn into one of the most interesting two-way centers in the NBA given his size (7'1", 250 pounds) and elite defensive potential.

Portland Trail Blazers: Donovan Clingan, C

Scoot Henderson would be a wishful thinking pick here, though the number of guards on this roster could limit his opportunities as long as Ja Morant, Damian Lillard and Jrue Holiday are all healthy.

Instead, a path is already in place for Donovan Clingan to make a leap for the Portland Trail Blazers.

The 7'2" center is locked in as the team's starting center after becoming a full-time starter last season. His minutes jumped from 19.8 as a rookie to 27.2 as a sophomore. There's still room for another leap, especially since Clingan has largely stayed out of foul trouble in his young career.

In the 21 games where he logged at least 30 minutes last season (32.9 on average), Clingan averaged 16.0 points, 14.1 rebounds, 2.9 assists and 2.0 blocks while shooting 58.6 percent overall and 41.3 percent from three on 75 total attempts.

Maxime Raynaud was a huge surprise for the Sacramento Kings last year, making a big impact despite being selected 42nd overall in the 2025 draft.

An injury to Domantas Sabonis opened up the starting center job for the 7'1" Raynaud, a role he thrived in. In a hot stretch to finish the year, the 23-year-old averaged 19.0 points and 8.6 rebounds while shooting 58.0 percent overall and 48.1 percent from three over his final 13 games.

Sabonis, 30, will be a name to watch in the trade market throughout the year as the young Kings look to build around players like Darius Acuff Jr. and Raynaud. If Sabonis is indeed moved, the second-year center could be in for a big season.

There may be some awkwardness when the San Antonio Spurs eventually bench veteran guard De'Aaron Fox in favor of Dylan Harper. It would absolutely be the right move for the franchise to make both now and in the future.

Harper logged just 22.6 minutes as a rookie, starting four of his 69 total games. Per 36 minutes of play, however, the No. 2 overall pick averaged 18.8 points, 5.4 rebounds, 6.1 assists, 1.2 steals and only 2.3 turnovers.

His play in the NBA Finals screamed future star, which is a path the Spurs need to carve out for him alongside Victor Wembanyama and Stephon Castle.

Toronto Raptors: Collin Murray-Boyles, F/C

Much of the attention this offseason has revolved around the on-again, off-again trade for Kawhi Leonard. The Toronto Raptors also have some young talent worth getting excited about.

Along with rookie Allen Graves and third-year guard Ja'Kobe Walter, Collin Murray-Boyles has a bright future in Toronto. The 9th overall pick in 2025, Murray-Boyles is already a highly skilled defender who has shown some good outside shooting and passing potential as well.

Now that Sandro Mamukelashvili has joined the Los Angeles Lakers, more frontcourt minutes could be available for Murray-Boyles, who only turned 21 this past summer.

Skill met opportunity down the stretch for Ace Bailey, as the No. 5 overall pick in the 2025 draft averaged 20.3 points, 5.5 rebounds, 2.5 assists and 1.5 blocks over the final 12 games of the season.

The Utah Jazz will look different this year, although that may not be a bad thing for Bailey's career arc. Yes, Darryn Peterson and Jaren Jackson Jr. will need their share of shots and touches, even though Cody Williams is gone and Utah will actually be trying to win games.

This means we should see a more polished, efficient version of Bailey, whether he ends up starting or not. The 6'9" wing has an ideal NBA frame and only turned 20 last month. It could be years until Bailey hits his peak, and outside of Peterson, he has the highest ceiling of anyone on the team.

Trae Young, Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr and AJ Dybantsa are all likely locked in as starters for the Washington Wizards next season. Tre Johnson, the No. 6 overall pick in 2025, could make his case as the final piece.

In the six games where he saw 30 minutes or more last season (32.4 average), the 6'5" shooting guard put up 16.8 points and 3.3 assists on 39.1 percent shooting from three. The Wizards finished in the bottom half of three-point makes and efficiency last season. Johnson's outside shooting ability could help improve that notable flaw.

The Wizards have a lot of young talent, creating an intriguing battle for rotation minutes now with veterans like Young, Davis, Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton on board.

articles.title: 2017 NBA Re-Draft Gives 76ers, Lakers the Ultimate Do-Overs
articles.summary: The 2017 NBA draft delivered superstars, champions and franchise cornerstones—just not in the spots everybody expected.
articles.body:
The 2017 NBA draft delivered superstars, champions and franchise cornerstones—just not in the spots everybody expected.

As members of that vaunted class get set to begin their 10th professional seasons, let's look back at where Jayson Tatum, Markelle Fultz, Donovan Mitchell and all the rest should have gone in the draft.

We're not at all concerned with team or system fit here. This is strictly a best-player-available exercise, though it gets complicated when trying to weigh career longevity against a shorter, higher peak. Yes, we're mostly talking about real-life No. 2 selection Lonzo Ball, but that balancing act will come up more than once.

Given what we know now, this is how the 2017 NBA Draft should have played out.

Jayson Tatum's Original Draft Position: No. 3

Jayson Tatum's five All-NBA nods are more than the rest of the 2017 draft class has combined. He was on a run of four straight top-six MVP finishes prior to missing most of last year while recovering from a torn Achilles.

In addition to career averages of 23.5 points, 7.9 rebounds and 3.9 assists, Tatum is the only player among his peers who qualifies as a two-way wing with first-option offensive chops. Even as trends have changed over the years, that's still the most valuable player type in the league.

It also doesn't hurt that Tatum is the only guy here who has checked the "best player on a championship team" box, setting him apart from a couple of other candidates with comparable counting stats.

Donovan Mitchell's Original Draft Position: No. 13

Donovan Mitchell is the only 2017 pick, besides Tatum, with an All-NBA First Team honor on his résumé. He actually has over 1,000 more career points than the guy who just came off the board ahead of him.

Even with Mitchell's other advantages over Tatum—more assists, steals, and made threes—he's not a threat to unseat the Boston Celtics superstar.

The issue is partly positional. Mitchell is a smallish guard who doesn't make much of an impact on defense and hasn't yet proven he's good enough offensively to take his team all the way to the top of the heap.

Though he's had some stellar playoff runs and been perhaps equally valuable during the regular season, Mitchell hasn't driven team success to the degree Tatum has.

Bam Adebayo's Original Draft Position: No. 14

After a pair of alpha scoring options in Tatum and Mitchell, versatile center Bam Adebayo is the no-brainer third pick in this re-draft.

Adebayo has been one of the league's preeminent defensive players throughout his career, bringing switchability across all five positions while still leading the class in total rebounds.

An excellent passer for his position, Adebayo actually ranks fifth among 2017 picks in total assists.

A six-time All-Defensive honoree whose three All-Star trips trail only Tatum and Mitchell, Adebayo can anchor an elite defense while functioning as a No. 2 option on the other end. He was integral to the Heat's Jimmy Butler-led stretch from 2020 to 2023, during which the team made three Eastern Conference Finals and two Finals.

Landing Spots for Top 5 Unsigned NBA Free Agents 🏀

Derrick White's Original Draft Position: No. 29

This is going to be a controversial choice because there's a much more star-worthy name still on the board at a similar position, but Derrick White has enough statistical and team-success support to make his case at No. 4.

First of all, White is among the best defensive players in the league right now and has been for the better part of his career. He has three All-Defensive nods, including last year's First Team honor. He has finished among the top 10 in DPOY voting every year since 2023-24. One of the greatest rim-protecting guards in NBA history, the 6'4" White has more swats than anyone but Jarrett Allen in the class.

Offensively, White isn't a first option, but his mid-career development as a three-point shooter makes him a great fit in any team's system. It doesn't hurt that he's also third among 2017 picks in assists.

Everyone will clamor for De'Aaron Fox here, but White leads him in career VORP and has driven far more wins over his career.

OG Anunoby's Original Draft Position: No. 23

It's hard to believe OG Anunoby has only made two All-Defensive teams. He somehow hasn't been a first-teamer once. Maybe it's the sheen of his recent championship run, complete with a Finals takeover, but his relatively empty individual trophy case feels like an oversight.

An ideally portable role player, Anunoby can defend every position on the floor and becomes even more valuable in the playoffs, when the need for a shutdown wing with elite length and strength is most pivotal. As physically sturdy as any forward in the league, Anunoby's lateral mobility sets him apart as a stopper.

No active player measures up to the "prime Kawhi Leonard" archetype on D, but Anunoby comes as close as anyone.

At 37.7 percent from long range for his career, Anunoby's offensive game is more than good enough to warrant the three-and-D label. He's not a shot-creator by any stretch, but he's spent most of his career as a player every team in the league would start and trust with heavy minutes.

De'Aaron Fox's Original Draft Position: No. 5

This may be a surprising fall for Fox, who slides past his original No. 5 spot and avoids landing with the Sacramento Kings. Given his trade request in 2024, he's probably not upset.

Of the many picks Sacramento would like to do over, Fox probably isn't one of them. Tough luck for the Kings.

Though he made just one All-Star team during his tenure with the squad, Fox was one of the organization's few bright spots over the past decade. He was the second-best player on the 2022-23 team that set a record for offensive efficiency and broke a 16-year playoff drought. He averaged at least 25.0 points per game in three different seasons.

Why does he slide behind White and Anunoby with a resumé like that? Fifteen players picked in 2017 have at least 4,000 career points. Fox rates dead last among them with a 51.9 effective field-goal percentage.

7. Minnesota Timberwolves: Lauri Markkanen

Lauri Markkanen's Original Draft Position: No. 7

Lauri Markkanen's last few seasons with the Utah Jazz, marked by early shutdowns and loads of missed games, make it hard to get a good feel for where he should rank in this class. Quietly, he had major durability issues before sitting so often in Utah, topping 65 games just once in his first five seasons with Chicago and Cleveland.

Whenever Markkanen has been available, he's been a tremendously efficient scorer. Toting a career hit rate of 37.0 percent from deep, the 7-footer is one of the few players his size who can reliably shoot the ball on the move. Paired with a dangerous catch-and-go game, Markkanen rounds out his profile with aggressive drives that force defenders into tough spots.

Last season, he set a career high with 6.4 free-throw attempts per game. At 87.1 percent from the foul line for his career, Markkanen makes those freebies count.

A one-time All-Star with a pair of 25-point-per-game seasons and a Most Improved Player award in 2022-23, Markkanen could elevate his profile by proving he can contribute to a Jazz team that is finally trying to win games.

Jarrett Allen's Original Draft Position: No. 20

Jarrett Allen is comfortably the second-best center in the 2017 class. Or, at least he's had the second-best career to date. Oklahoma City Thunder big man Isaiah Hartenstein took a while to get going but is probably the superior player at the moment.

With over 200 more blocked shots than anyone else in the class, Allen is easily 2017's top rim-protecting force. Only Adebayo has a higher rebound total, though he's logged over 2,000 more career minutes than Allen, leaving little doubt as to the class' best per-minute board man.

A one-time All-Star with three top-12 finishes in DPOY voting, Allen has been a reliable and efficient double-digit scorer en route to career marks of 13.1 points and 9.2 rebounds per game. He's never been a marquee name, but we're reaching the point of the re-draft where "quality starter" is good enough.

Isaiah Hartenstein's Original Draft Position: No. 43

Isaiah Hartenstein probably wouldn't be among the top 30 picks in a re-draft of the 2017 class a few years ago. It took him until 2018-19 to see his first NBA action and until the midpoint of the 2023-24 season to earn a regular starting role.

That breakout year with the New York Knicks led to Hartenstein's move to the Oklahoma City Thunder, where he's been an indispensable part of two straight 60-win seasons and the 2024-25 championship.

A physical interior defender who averages 12.1 rebounds per 36 minutes, Hartenstein contributes on offense with his vastly underrated passing and work on the offensive boards. With great touch on short floaters, he's also become a dangerous threat as a roll man.

Right now, he's better than every center in the class but Adebayo. Allen went ahead of him only because of the greater volume of quality years.

Josh Hart's Original Draft Position: No. 30

A dominant transition threat and one of the best rebounding wings of his era, Josh Hart is yet another glue guy coming off the board in the re-draft lottery.

Hart's rugged, all-out style has resulted in more than a few injuries, but no one would consider telling him to turn down the intensity. A team with Hart on the floor just plays harder and more aggressively, if only to keep up with him.

Though mostly known for his on-the-margins contributions, Hart has somewhat surprisingly posted double-digit scoring averages four times, including each of the last two seasons with the Knicks. His three-point shot comes and goes, but inconsistency from beyond the arc shouldn't overshadow his championship-vetted two-way play.

Dillon Brooks' Original Draft Position: No. 45

Many advanced metrics despise Dillon Brooks, mostly because of his career 42.1 percent field-goal percentage and limited facilitation skills. He's actually dead last among 2017 draftees in career VORP.

But you don't wind up ranking 10th in the class in total minutes and ninth in points by accident.

Brooks carved out a role for himself by establishing a physical, "right up to the line and sometimes over it" level of defensive aggression. He's an irritant, an instigator and a wildly overconfident blowhard on the floor. And it works.

Even if he's inefficient, takes bad shots and sometimes pokes the wrong bears, Brooks has made a habit of helping teams win and watching them struggle after he's gone. From Memphis to Houston to Phoenix, Brooks delivers grit and tone-setting toughness at every stop.

John Collins' Original Draft Position: No. 19

Early on, John Collins looked like a potential future star. As a 21-year-old with the Atlanta Hawks, the bouncy forward put up 19.5 points and 9.8 rebounds while dabbling as a three-point shooter, hitting 34.8 percent of his 2.6 attempts per game.

The following year, Collins was only healthy for 41 games but averaged 21.6 points and 10.1 rebounds while canning 40.1 percent of his threes on even higher volume.

Though he has continued to score plenty while shooting over 50.0 percent from the field in every year of his career, Collins never quite delivered on the promise of those early years. Still a starter who offers real stretch at the 4, Collins is now a defensively iffy role player whose impact mostly depends on whether or not his catch-and-shoot threes are falling.

Malik Monk's Original Draft Position: No. 11

Malik Monk's career got off to a brutal start, as the top-10 pick shot under 40.0 percent from the field in his first two seasons before having his third ended early with an indefinite suspension for violating the NBA and NBPA Anti-Drug Program.

Nearly slipping out of the league seemed to serve as a wakeup call.

Upon returning, Monk became a better three-point shooter and averaged double figures on the way to two straight top-five finishes in Sixth Man voting with the Sacramento Kings in 2022-23 and 2023-24.

Viewed mostly as a scoring guard early on, Monk also added real playmaking dimensions with the Kings, averaging over 5.0 assists per game in 2023-24 and 2024-25. He's currently seventh in the 2017 draft class in total dimes and sixth in made triples.

Luke Kennard's Original Draft Position: No. 12

Sixty-one players have made at least 1,000 threes since 2017-18. Luke Kennard is easily the most accurate sniper in that group.

At 44.2 percent for his career, Kennard has run away with the accuracy crown over the last nine years, topping second-place finisher Stephen Curry's relatively modest 40.9 percent.

Despite his superpower as a long-range gunner, Kennard has bounced between six teams and has almost never held a regular starting role. He's not much of a defender but deserves credit for being an underrated facilitator at the 2.

He falls a bit from his original draft spot at No. 12, but Kennard is a true specialist who has mostly delivered on expectations.

Kyle Kuzma's Original Draft Position: No. 27

If Kyle Kuzma had stayed on the path he established during his first season when he finished fourth in Rookie of the Year and ninth in Sixth Man, he'd probably rank higher in our re-draft.

That version of Kuzma was a defense-first role player who didn't dribble much, played with great energy and still managed to average 16.1 points and 6.3 rebounds per game.

As he matured and changed teams a couple of times, Kuzma morphed into a somewhat unserious, empty scorer. It didn't help that he played his prime years with the aimless Washington Wizards, which enabled some of his worst instincts.

Still, Kuzma's size on the wing and (inefficient) scoring ability were enough to get him the fifth-most career minutes in the class to date. He's also fifth in total points, despite an effective field-goal percentage that ranks 14th among the top 15 scorers among 2017 draftees.

Lonzo Ball's Original Draft Position: No. 2

This is a long way to fall for someone who was briefly one of the top role players in the league, but Lonzo Ball is effectively out of the NBA at age 28 and has missed approximately two and a half seasons due to injury. Though his peak was relatively high, Ball simply didn't play enough to ascend in the re-draft order.

Ball put up a career-best 7.2 assists per game as a rookie with the Lakers. That was when he still profiled as more of a true point guard. It became clear that Ball's early-career shooting limitations and underwhelming athletic burst better suited him for a role as a secondary creator.

Across three seasons with the New Orleans Pelicans and Chicago Bulls, he shined as a catch-and-shoot gunner, ace connective passer, elite transition trigger and disruptive off-ball defender.

For a brief moment, Ball was the kind of gap-filling starter every team craved. That period just didn't last long enough.

Jonathan Isaac's Original Draft Position: No. 6

It wouldn't be unfair to call Jonathan Isaac the forward version of Lonzo Ball—a player with clear niche skills who made a major impact on winning until injuries derailed everything.

A 6'10", defense-first project out of Florida State, Isaac flashed a ton of disruption and rebounding prowess across his first three seasons. Like Ball, multiple knee injuries cost Isaac two full years in what should have been his early prime and effectively put him on a permanent minutes limit. He hasn't averaged more than 15.8 minutes per game since 2019-20.

Routinely clocking in above the 90th percentile in Defensive Estimated Plus/Minus, Isaac continues to provide serious stopping power in his limited role.

Monte Morris' Original Draft Position: No. 51

For a five-season stretch from 2018-19 to 2022-23, Monte Morris was one of the most underrated point guards in the league.

After playing just 25 total minutes as a rookie, he ascended to a starring sixth-man role with the Nuggets during his second campaign, averaging 10.4 points and 3.6 assists while canning 41.4 percent of his threes. Morris posted similar numbers in each of his next two seasons in Denver, then jumped into a full-time starting role to relieve the injured Jamal Murray in 2021-22.

Things fell off a bit after Morris left the Nuggets, but he totes career averages of 9.4 points and 3.6 assists, with a sterling 38.8 percent from three.

Luke Kornet's Original Draft Position: Undrafted

Luke Kornet's best season came in 2024-25 with the Boston Celtics, when he played a career-high 73 games and averaged 4.6 offensive boards per 36 minutes, stats that would have shocked observers who saw the 7'1" center come into the league billed mostly as a perimeter threat.

Undrafted in 2017, Kornet took over half of his field-goal attempts from beyond the arc across each of his first four seasons before effectively abandoning his jumper and focusing on using his size around the rim.

A good illustration of the change: Kornet shot 38.2 percent from the field on a three-heavy diet with the Knicks but upped that to 65.4 percent in five seasons with the Celtics after shelving the deep ball.

A career backup who now plays spot minutes behind Victor Wembanyama in San Antonio, Kornet has carved out a solid career after watching 60 players get picked ahead of him in 2017.

Bonus points for being one of the funnier interview subjects in the league.

20. Portland Trail Blazers: Chris Boucher

Chris Boucher's Original Draft Position: Undrafted

Only six players in the 2017 draft class have at least 300 blocks and 300 made threes in their careers. Chris Boucher is one of them.

Though the undrafted big man is nowhere near the overall impact level of the other five—Jayson Tatum, Derrick White, OG Anunoby, John Collins and Kyle Kuzma—he deserves credit for filling an in-demand role over the last nine years.

Boucher also holds the distinction of winning championships with two different teams in his first two seasons. He played a single game on a two-way contract for the title-winning 2017-18 Warriors, then collected a second ring with the Raptors the following season.

The best of Boucher's nine seasons came in 2020-21 with the Raps, when he averaged 13.6 points and 6.7 rebounds while posting a 51.4/38.3/78.8 shooting split, earning the eighth-most votes for Sixth Man of the Year.

Zach Collins' Original Draft Position: No. 10

Never a regular starter, Zach Collins still managed to put up 9.7 points and 5.2 rebounds per game during his best seasons with the San Antonio Spurs from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

General defensive shakiness and a lack of heft have consigned Collins to a mostly offensive role. He's made at least 40 threes in three different seasons of his career. He might have developed into an even more effective weapon in his mid-20s if the ankle injury that cost him all of 2020-21 hadn't sapped some of his bounce.

At this point in the draft, a somewhat stretchy big man with career averages of 15.3 points, 9.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists per 36 minutes is about as good as it gets.

Thomas Bryant's Original Draft Position: No. 42

Thomas Bryant peaked early, putting up 10.5 points and 6.3 rebounds per game in 72 appearances (53 starts) as a 21-year-old in his second season. Though he logged only 56 total games over the next two years, Bryant's efficiency around the basket, solid rebounding and quiet accuracy on low-volume deep shooting made him a very useful starting center.

Bryant bounced around after that, landing on six teams over his nine-year career. Back with the Cavaliers and slated for a second-unit role, the 29-year-old is still a viable energetic reserve who drags opposing centers out of the paint with the threat of his three-point stroke.

Dennis Smith Jr.'s Original Draft Position: No. 9

A fifth-place finish in Rookie of the Year voting suggested that the hyper-athletic Dennis Smith Jr. was on track to become a two-way star.

Though he salvaged his career by morphing into one of the better on-ball defenders at the guard position, Smith never matched his first-year averages of 15.2 points and 5.2 assists per game.

In fact, the Dallas Mavericks dealt him to the Knicks midway through his second season—not exactly a great sign for a lottery pick who'd been pretty productive as a rookie.

Poor long-range shooting, some ill-timed injuries and an overall offensive game that just wasn't complete enough combined to push DSJ out of the league in 2024 after 326 career games.

Markelle Fultz's Original Draft Position: No. 1

A mysterious shoulder injury may or may not have contributed to a case of the shooting yips and a crisis of confidence, which effectively erased the elite draft pedigree Markelle Fultz was supposed to bring to the league.

We may never get clarity on the breakdown of his skills. Suffice it to say, there were mental and physical factors involved.

Despite his wildly disappointing start, Fultz built a modest career after joining the Magic in 2019-20. He averaged 11.6 points, 4.8 assists and 1.2 steals in five years with Orlando, starting 149 of the 201 games he played. Though he never managed to straighten out his jumper (career 27.5 percent from deep), Fultz used his size and passing acumen to produce like a low-end starter when healthy.

Unfortunately, the 28-year-old's time in the NBA may be done. He secured a 10-day deal with the Raptors this season but remains unsigned late in the 2026 offseason.

Simone Fontecchio's Original Draft Position: Undrafted

Technically a member of the 2017 draft class, Italian forward Simone Fontecchio opted to start his career in Europe after being passed over by the NBA. Since debuting at age 27 for the Utah Jazz in 2022-23, his reliable outside shot and underrated fake-and-go game have made him a useful rotation weapon.

Fontecchio's best work came in 2023-24 when he averaged 10.5 points and 3.7 rebounds while hitting 40.1 percent of his threes. A midseason trade that year sent him from Utah to Detroit, where he enjoyed a mini late-season breakout.

The 15.4 points he averaged over 16 games for the Pistons down the stretch didn't hold up, but Fontecchio logged 70 games for the Heat last season and scored 8.5 points in only 16.8 minutes per game. It's not too late for him to put up serious numbers if he ever lands a bigger role.

26. Portland Trail Blazers: Justin Jackson

Justin Jackson's Original Draft Position: No. 15

It might surprise you to learn that Justin Jackson hung around through the 2023-24 season. Well, he technically lasted that long. The real-life No. 15 pick appeared in two games for the Wolves that year.

Jackson's final few seasons were quiet enough to be completely overlooked, to the point that many assumed he was out of the league earlier than he was. But he was noisier early on.

He started 41 of the 68 games he played for the Kings as a rookie. The 6'8" wing was a rotation regular through the 2020-21 season, split between the Thunder and Bucks. At his best during his second season, Jackson averaged 7.2 points, 2.6 rebounds and 1.2 assists on a 44.7/35.5/78.5 shooting split across 81 games.

Frank Ntilikina's Original Draft Position: No. 8

Frank Ntilikina could disrupt on defense right away and started to flash capable shooting chops a bit too late to salvage his career. Knicks fans surely remember the 47.9 percent he shot in 33 games during the 2020-21 season, if only because that level of accuracy stood out so starkly against what he'd done up to that point in his career.

A solid season with the Mavs in 2021-22 saw the French guard knock down 34.2 percent of his triples on increased per-minute volume, but poor two-point finishing resulted in the fifth straight season shooting under 40.0 percent from the field.

Ntilikina ranks 24th in total minutes, 22nd in steals and 21st in assists in the class. Do not ask where he ranks in field-goal percentage (it's 54th).

Tony Bradley's Original Draft Position: No. 28

A lack of mobility and scoring touch prevented Tony Bradley from ever settling in as a rotation mainstay, but he's been a highly productive reserve when deployed against lineups that don't expose his limitations.

Across 234 games, Bradley averages 14.3 points, 12.5 rebounds and 1.6 blocks per 36 minutes.

Credit the big man for fighting his way back into the NBA after slipping down to the G League in 2023-24. Nobody's going to say the 14 contests he played for the Eastern Conference champion Pacers in 2024-25 (plus 11 postseason appearances) were the reason they advanced so far, but it's telling that Bradley saw real action for a high-level team so recently.

Sterling Brown's Original Draft Position: No. 46

We've reached the point where anyone who played in a rotation is fair game, so Sterling Brown lands just inside the top 30 after going 46th in real life.

An undersized wing who entered the league with the pre-championship Milwaukee Bucks, Brown averaged at least 14.0 minutes per contest across his first three years—the last two of which saw teammate Giannis Antetokounmpo named MVP.

Brown's exit from Milwaukee was ill-timed. The Bucks won the title in 2020-21, immediately after he left for the Rockets. At least Brown put up a career year in Houston, averaging 8.2 points and draining 42.3 percent of his threes over 51 games, including 14 starts.

Josh Jackson's Original Draft Position: No. 4

Things never quite came together for Jackson, a theoretical two-way wing whose 6'8" size and perceived versatility convinced the Suns he was worth a top-five pick.

Jackson averaged 13.1 points as a rookie, but the scoring inefficiency (41.7 percent from the field; 26.3 percent from deep) that would define his career rendered those points empty.

It seemed Jackson might enjoy a second act when he played 62 games for the Pistons in 2020-21, scoring 13.4 points per game and showing more passing chops than he ever had before. Because of poor shooting and immaturity off the court, he was out of the league by 2022 and hasn't made it back.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: Updated Top 25 WNBA Player Rankings Ahead of 2026 Playoffs
articles.summary: With just one week left in the WNBA regular season, it's time for one final update to our top 25 player rankings ahead of the playoffs.
articles.body:
With just one week left in the WNBA regular season, it's time for one final update to our top 25 player rankings ahead of the playoffs.

These rankings are based entirely on what players have done this season. Availability matters, too. Players who have missed significant time and played fewer than 50 percent of their team's games won't be ranked, which leaves players like Kelsey Plum and Napheesa Collier out of consideration.

We also place a lot of value on two-way impact. Offensive production matters, but so does what a player brings defensively and how they contribute to winning basketball. Though, of course, if you're having a historic season on one side of the ball, you can make up for this.

With that said, let's get into the final rankings.

At just 22 years old, Leite has already done something no other player in league history has. She's generating 22.4 points per game out of pick-and-roll, according to Synergy Sports.

Leite is almost impossible to keep in front of ball screens. She gets two feet in the paint at-will, whether it's blowing by her defender for an easy layup, drawing fouls at a historic rate or forcing the defense to help and opening up passing windows. Her assist rate also jumped from 22.4 percent to 42.5 percent this season.

The next step for Leite is building on the shooting improvements she made this year by increasing her 3-point volume—specifically off the catch. It would also be nice if she could make some strides defensively, even if she's unlikely to ever be a positive on that end.

Iriafen is the third-best player on a team that is eight games over .500 in just her second season, and she deserves a ton of credit for that. Iriafen dominates on the glass, runs the floor hard, scores efficiently around the rim and is a very good team defender.

Before the Olympic break, Iriafen had a five-game stretch with at least 18 points and 10 rebounds—tied for the third-longest such streak in WNBA history and the longest by a player under 25 years old.

What keeps Iriafen from ranking higher is her struggles as a primary rim protector and as a shooter from almost everywhere on the floor.

A year ago, Mabrey was firmly in the low-efficiency, shot-chucker bucket in Connecticut. Now, in Toronto, she's put together the most efficient pull-up 3-point shooting season (40.4% on 4.4 attempts per game) by any player not named Kelsey Mitchell.

Toronto's season was plagued by injuries, and even when healthy, the team struggled to beat good opponents. But Mabrey has flourished under Sandy Brondello, putting together a career year as a driver, playmaker, shot creator and movement shooter.

It's been fun to watch Williams back in her natural scoring role next to Olivia Miles. Her mid-range scoring has been elite as always, while the playmaking relief allows her to really lock in on the ball defensively.

Though, Williams hasn't been quite as effective since Napheesa Collier returned, averaging just 10.9 points on 41.4 percent shooting from the field over her last 12 games. That has pushed her down a bit and out of All-WNBA consideration.

Last month, Ogwumike announced she would retire from the WNBA at the end of the season, but if she wanted to keep playing, she could continue performing at an All-Star level for a couple more years.

Ogwumike is averaging 17.2 points, 8.9 rebounds and 3.0 assists on 60 percent true shooting. She's shot over 50 percent from two in every season of her career—a feat nobody else has accomplished—while also developing into a serious shooter over the back half of her career.

Burton is the best two-way point guard in the WNBA, and it's not much of a debate. She's elite defensively, shoots threes at a solid level, draws fouls and almost always makes the right decision with the ball.

Burton is averaging 6.4 assists to just 0.8 turnovers per game since the All-Star break, including a two-game stretch against Connecticut and New York where she recorded 20 assists without a single turnover.

Citron's 3-point shooting has regressed by more than 10 percent since her rookie season, but that hasn't stopped her from improving in almost every other area.

She's an outstanding driver, reading angles incredibly well, changes speeds and uses ball pickups at perfect spots to score efficiently around the rim. Citron's also a great cutter with an innate feel for off-ball movement and high-level wing defender who has taken on more lead-guard responsibilities in the process.

Citron has nearly doubled her pick-and-roll volume, going from 5.5 pick-and-rolls per game in 2025 (0.87 points per possession) to 9.7 this season (0.96).

Jones is the best shooting center in women's basketball history. This season, she's knocking down nearly 40 percent of her threes on a career-high 4.7 attempts per game.

On top of that, there aren't many players at her size who can handle the ball like she can. Head coach Chris DeMarco has found creative ways to use Jones in inverted ball screens, and it's tough to stop.

What keeps Jones from being an All-WNBA player like she was in 2024 (and the many years prior) is her defensive decline and inconsistent effort on that end. New York's defensive rating is 3.9 points worse per 100 possessions with her on the court compared to when she's off.

It's been a disastrous season for the Phoenix Mercury, but make no mistake: Thomas is still very good at basketball. She's averaging 14.2 points, 7.7 rebounds and 8.4 assists per game on 51.2 percent shooting from the field.

However, she's taken a step back defensively and hasn't been quite as dominant as a ball-screen creator, evident by her 6.1 percent drop from 2025 in efficiency out of pick-and-roll.

There are questions to be had about Shepard's defense and impact on playoff basketball, but don't let that cloud what she's done for the Dallas Wings this season.

She's one of the most unique stars we've ever seen, with her combination of passing, rebounding, screening and open-court creation at 6'4". Shepard is the perfect offensive fit next to Paige Bueckers, allowing her to maximize her premier off-ball skill set.

Reese isn't your conventional star, but she impacts winning in so many different ways. She's the best rebounder in WNBA history, a lock for an All-Defensive team and an elite transition scorer who consistently turns defense into offense.

Is she an efficient interior scorer? No. Can she shoot? No, absolutely not. Yet, she makes everyone around her better and shows up when it matters most.

Atlanta's defense is 14.2 points better per 100 with her on the court compared to when she's off, while only being marginally worse offensively (-1.9).

Howard went back to play under Cheryl Reeve, got to run ball screens with rookie Olivia Miles and somehow discovered the Fountain of Youth.

At 35 years old, she's the best play finisher in basketball, ranking first in 2-point field goals out of pick-and-roll (72) and third as a cutter (53). Howard is also an elite defender, with versatility in ball screens and the athleticism and length to be just as impactful in help.

It might be tough for Indiana to get three All-WNBA players if they finish outside of the top three, but Boston is right there in the mix.

She went from shooting 26.2 percent from three (17 made) over her first three seasons to 40.8 percent (40 made and counting) this year. There's not much she can't do offensively now.

Boston hasn't been quite as elite defensively this year, but there's no doubt she's the most valuable defender on the Fever. Opponents shoot 6.6 percent worse at the rim with Boston on the court, compared to when she's off.

This might seem low, but it has more to do with other players leveling up their games than any decline from Gray. You're really just splitting hairs in the No. 7-13 range.

This season, Gray has posted career highs in points (19.3) and 2-point percentage (54.4%), while also being a well-above-average wing defender.

But for as good as she is as an interior scorer, her shooting hasn't been at the 2025 level. Against playoff teams, she's shooting 31.9 percent from the mid-range and 30.1 percent from three. Those numbers jump to 65.2 percent and 37.2 percent, respectively, against non-playoff teams.

Williams' developmental arc since entering the WNBA has been truly insane. She was once a defense-only specialist who was scared to take threes, and now the defense is still just as elite while she's become someone teams have to respect from beyond the arc.

Golden State has so much depth that Williams only plays 24.8 minutes per game, yet she still averages 14.3 points. If you adjust that to per-36 minutes, she's at 20.8 points, right there with Allisha Gray (21.1) and Jackie Young (21.0).

Williams over Gray in these rankings might be a hot take, but Golden State did go 3-0 in the regular-season matchups against Atlanta, with Williams outplaying Gray head-to-head.

2026 Stats: 18.1 PTS, 3.1 REB, 2.2 AST, 41.7% 3P

It's completely insane that McBride wasn't an All-Star. She's the best movement shooter in the league and a very good driver who uses her gravity as a downhill creator and cutter. On top of that, McBride should be in the All-Defense conversation.

She's on pace to become the third player in WNBA history to shoot 50 percent from two, 40 percent from three and 90 percent from the free-throw line while averaging at least 1.5 steals per game in a season, joining Napheesa Collier in 2025 and Brandy Reed in 2000.

9. Shakira Austin, C, Washington Mystics

2026 Stats: 16.9 PTS, 9.4 REB, 2.5 AST, 48.9% FG

In our last player rankings article in June, Austin was left out of our Top 25. Now, we're making the case for her to be a second-team All-WNBA player. So, what changed?

It's not like Austin was having a bad first half of the season. Washington was winning games, and she was one of their most impactful players. But the turnovers were an issue, and her efficiency was inconsistent from game to game.

Since the start of July, though, there's a real case that Austin has been the best player in the league outside of A'ja Wilson. She's averaging 19.8 points and 9.6 rebounds on 51.9 percent shooting from the field while anchoring the No. 2 defense over that 22-game stretch.

The way Austin moves and attacks downhill at her size is insane, so Washington has started to weaponize these skills as a pick-and-roll creator. Since the All-Star break, she's ran 2.3 ball screens per game for 1.22 points per possession, compared to 1.4 for 0.54 PPP prior to that.

2026 Stats: 18.9 PTS, 4.4 REB, 6.6 AST, 48.3% FG

If it weren't for Jackie Young's slow start over her first seven games (10.1 points on under 35 percent shooting), she'd be averaging 20.8 points and 6.8 assists on 59 percent shooting from two and 41.4 percent from three.

The shot creation is elite, the finishing is unreal, she has the best floater in the league and her ability to create advantages as a passer is high-level, too. But the entire body of work and high-level two-way impact still matter, giving Howard (two-way impact) and Bueckers (body of work) a slight edge for us.

2026 Stats: 18.3 PTS, 3.8 REB, 3.6 AST, 41.0% FG

Howard is one of the best shooters in the league, an unquestioned top-two wing defender in the world, an improved 2-point scorer and almost never turns the ball over.

Here's the list of players in WNBA history to post at least a 3% steal rate, 2% block rate and shoot 35% from three on at least two attempts per game:

Tamika Catchings, four times – finished top five in MVP every season

2026 Stats: 20.5 PTS, 4.1 REB, 5.9 AST, 50.6% FG

It only took Bueckers until her second season to lead Dallas back to the postseason, thanks to her outrageous offensive impact.

She might go down as the greatest mid-range scorer in basketball history, on top of being one of the best off-ball movers and processors we've ever seen. Oh yeah, she's also taking pull-up threes now and knocking them down at a near 40 percent clip.

It's crazy, but Bueckers' biggest flaw is herself. Her passiveness at times is puzzling, and her willingness to get to the rim has gotten worse, if anything. As a rookie, 18.4% of her shots in the half court came at the rim—that number is down to just 12.7% in 2026. We've also seen more fouls than ever before in the WNBA, yet Bueckers' free-throw rate has only increased by 5 percent.

2026 Stats: 22.5 PTS, 3.9 REB, 8.4 AST, 45.6% FG

Clark is the engine behind the greatest offensive team in WNBA history.

She sees everything as a pick-and-roll and transition creator, and her gravity allows her to create more efficient looks for her teammates than anyone else in the league. And now, she's added a legitimate floater and the pull-up jumper has started to fall consistently, too.

Since the start of July, Clark is shooting 49.1 percent on pull-up twos (28-57) and 43.6 percent on pull-up threes (48-110).

When Clark has the pull-up three going, teams have to sell out even harder on her jumpers. Well, but she's got the in-between game going, too, and the finishing is elite. When all of that is on, there's no answer and that's been the case for a couple months.

2026 Stats: 25.0 PTS, 1.7 REB, 2.8 AST, 51.3% FG

Kelsey Mitchell is the best small-guard scorer in basketball history (under 5'9" in the WNBA and 6'2" in the NBA). There's an argument for Kelsey Plum, Jalen Brunson, Allen Iverson and 2017 Isaiah Thomas, but none of those players can score from everywhere and in every play type quite like Mitchell.

Here's the full picture of her 2026 season:

57.1% effective field-goal percentage out of PnR — No. 2 in the league

I see the argument for Clark over Mitchell because of her impact in more areas, but Mitchell has been the better player in the biggest games. Her 62.7 percent true-shooting is nearly 10 percentage points higher than Clark against playoff teams.

3. Breanna Stewart, PF, New York Liberty

2026 Stats: 20.4 PTS, 8.1 REB, 3.2 AST, 46.5% FG

Breanna Stewart was once a 37.5% 3-point shooter over a four-year stretch. Now, she's shooting 25% from three, and she's still a top-five player in the world.

That's because there are so many other ways for her to impact the game. She's an elite transition player, cutter, foul-drawer and passer who can score as both a roller and ball-handler out of ball screens.

Stewart also dominates on the glass and can defend almost any position. She's one of five players in the league averaging at least a steal and block per game.

2026 Stats: 19.7 PTS, 4.6 REB, 6.0 AST, 49.5% FG

Miles is the best player on the best team in the league… as a rookie. If A'ja Wilson weren't the greatest player of all time, Miles would probably be the second rookie to win MVP in the WNBA and the fourth to win in basketball history.

She's already the most dynamic passer and driver in the world. Miles can make any pass from virtually any spot on the court, while getting to the rim whenever she wants and finishing with either hand better than any guard in the league.

She's not always guarded like the 40 percent 3-point shooter she is, but she's making defenses pay when they go under screens. Over her last 19 games, Miles is shooting 42.2 percent from three on 5.0 attempts per game, compared to 32.8 percent on 3.4 attempts over her first 19.

Just keep in mind, this is the worst she's going to be.

2026 Stats: 26.0 PTS, 9.4 REB, 3.2 AST, 52.3% FG

Wilson is the best player in the WNBA, and there's a larger gap between her and the field than any other major sports league in the United States (and maybe the world).

Wilson is averaging 26.0 points, 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists and 2.0 blocks on 54.3 percent shooting from two and 39.8 percent from three.

There's nothing she can't do. Wilson can score on the interior, create her own shot in the mid-range, hit catch-and-shoot jumpers, pass, rebound and defend at a high level.

Las Vegas is 25.9 points better per 100 possessions with Wilson on the court than when she's off. That's the difference between the best team in the league when she plays and the worst team when she sits.

articles.title: LeBron James’ son Bronny James gets stern warning as his fight for a playing spot looms
articles.summary: NBA News: Bronny James is staring down the most pressure-packed stretch of his short NBA career, and the warnings keep piling up. The Los Angeles Lakers guarant.
articles.body: Bronny James is staring down the most pressure-packed stretch of his short NBA career, and the warnings keep piling up. The Los Angeles Lakers guaranteed his salary for this season, but that security comes with a catch: earn a real role, or watch the roster math turn against him fast.As the training camp is closing in, the message coming out of the Lakers' orbit is pretty clear. James has flashed the tools people keep pointing to, yet none of that matters if he can't turn brief bursts into something consistent.Bronny James gets stern warning ahead of new NBA seasonSince his father, LeBron James, left Los Angeles this summer, Bronny has been a subject of discussion. Every scoreless stretch gets picked apart, every shooting slump becomes a storyline, and now comes pointed calls for him to reshape his entire game plan.Writing for LakeShowLife.com, Tyler Watts laid out what the Lakers actually need from James this year, holding up Oklahoma City's Cason Wallace as the blueprint.“The Los Angeles Lakers showed faith in Bronny James this summer, but they need him to crack the rotation to stick long-term,” Watts wrote.Wallace forged his role through tenacious perimeter defense, smart spacing and timely playmaking rather than shot creation, and Watts believes James has to copy that formula to survive final cuts.“Bronny isn’t going to be an on-ball creator in LA. He must embrace the role Cason Wallace has played for the Oklahoma City Thunder as an undersized guard who plays stout defense, spaces the floor, and can create offense when needed. The Lakers should feed James tape of Wallace and convince him this is his path to playing time.”James already shows pieces of that defensive foundation. He has held up guarding smaller, quicker ball handlers in G League.Head coach JJ Redick pointed to Indiana's TJ McConnell and Miami's Davion Mitchell last year as the type of player James should study, and Watts figures that advice still holds now. If James turns into a connector guard who guards point of attack and complements Luka Doncic or Austin Reaves in the backcourt, extra playing time tends to follow on its own.Bronny James has to fight for playing spotTurns out James isn't the only one sweating roster decisions this fall. The Lakers loaded up on guards over the offseason, and three names are now competing for one open spot: Dalton Knecht, Jaden Hardy and James himself.Hardy arrived through the Deandre Ayton trade and owns a career 38.6% clip from three, though his defense and playmaking still trail what a rotation piece needs to offer. Knecht has slid the other direction since his rookie season, watching his minutes and shooting numbers shrink each year, and the front office has to settle his team option before Halloween.Of the three, James still looks like the safest bet to stick. The Lakers guaranteed his salary early in the offseason, a move made just before LeBron left the franchise, and that alone signals some patience from the front office. His production improved too. Across 42 games in 2025, the guard averaged 2.9 points, 1.2 assists and 0.5 rebounds in 8.9 minutes a night, modest numbers on paper, but his three-point shooting climbed from 28.1% to 38.6%, real growth from a player once written off as a name-only draft pick.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Kawhi Leonard Isn't 'Championship Chasing,' Reflects on Trade to Raptors from Clippers in New Video
articles.summary: Now that he is officially back with the Toronto Raptors, Kawhi Leonard has reflected on the process that led to his return to the team he won a championship with during the 2018-19 season.
articles.body:
Now that he is officially back with the Toronto Raptors, Kawhi Leonard has reflected on the process that led to his return to the team he won a championship with during the 2018-19 season.

In a new video released by the Raptors (starts at 4:00 mark), Leonard explains he's not "championship chasing" at this latter stage of his career.

"I'm not really championship chasing, trying to find the best team that can win," he said. "You know, I didn't want to put on a thousand jerseys. The city took a liking to my family. I took a liking to the city. Really enjoyed it. My son was born here, and you know, he's been asking me forever when he's gonna come back. So, now he's back, and he's able to see it rather than me tell him the great stories that happened."

Landing Spots for Top 5 Unsigned NBA Free Agents 🏀

Even though Leonard isn't only pursuing titles, it's hard not to look at what his addition means for the Raptors in their quest to get back to being a championship contender in the Eastern Conference.

Toronto improved by 16 wins from 2024-25 to 2025-26, finishing with a 46-36 record last season. It was the team's most victories in a season since 2019-20.

Leading the way for that improvement was Scottie Barnes, who made the All-Star team for the second time in three years and finished fifth in Defensive Player of the Year voting.

It's not a surprise at one point in the video, Leonard said the Raptors are "his team" referencing Barnes and he wants to do "whatever it takes to help" in whatever ways he can.

A healthy Leonard can be a game-changer for the Raptors and the Eastern Conference. He is coming off one of the best regular-season performances of his career, averaging 27.9 points on 50.5 percent shooting, 6.4 rebounds and 3.6 assists per game in 2025-26.

The most encouraging stat from Leonard last season was 65 games played, his second-most since 2017-18. If the Raptors get that many games from him in 2026-27, they have the pieces to challenge the top-tier teams in the East like the New York Knicks, Philadelphia 76ers and Boston Celtics.

articles.title: La reivindicación de Causeur: "El Real Madrid debería retirar los números de algunas leyendas"
articles.standfirst: El exjugador es partidario de que el club cuelgue las camisetas de Rudy Fernández, Felipe Reyes y Sergio Llull
articles.summary: El exjugador es partidario de que el club cuelgue las camisetas de Rudy Fernández, Felipe Reyes y Sergio Llull
articles.body: Fabien Causeur ha vuelto a abrir en las redes sociales un debate recurrente entre los aficionados del Real Madrid: la retirada de dorsales que han vestido jugadores míticos de la sección. El club blanco, pese a las leyendas que han vestido esa camiseta, sólo tiene colgada del techo la de Fernando Martín, fallecido en accidente de tráfico en 1989. El exjugador francés ha escrito en sus redes sociales: "Creo que el Real Madrid debería retirar los números de algunas leyendas. O por lo menos no dejar a otro jugador usar algunos números. No me puedo imaginar a alguien llevar el 23 después de Sergi [Llull], el 9 de Felipe [Reyes] o el 5 de Rudy [Fernández]. Hablo por los que más me han impactado". Después de siete temporadas en el club blanco, Causeur parece una voz autorizada para hablar del asunto. Ganó 14 títulos con dos Euroligas, cuatro Ligas Endesa, dos Copas del Rey y seis Supercopas Endesa y salió el equipo en 2024 después de dejar una profunda huella en los aficionados y en el seno del equipo. Lo cierto es que han sido tantos los jugadores ilustres que han pasado por el Madrid que habría que retirar numerosos dorsales. el 4 de Wayne Brabender, el 5 de Rudy Fernández y Vicente Ramos, el 6 de Fernando Romay, el 9 de Felipe Reyes, el 11 de Juan Antonio Corbalán y Arvydas Sabonis, el 12 de Rafa Rullán, el 13 de Clifford Luyk y Sergio Rodríguez, el 15 de Mirza Delibasic... Pese a la reclamación de un ídolo reciente como es Causeur, no parece que el Madrid vaya a cambiar una filosofía que se mantiene en el tiempo y cuya única excepción es la del malogrado Fernando Martín.

articles.standfirst: España asciende tres puestos y se queda sólo por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia, finalistas en el torneo
articles.summary: España asciende tres puestos y se queda sólo por detrás de Estados Unidos y Francia, finalistas en el torneo
articles.body: Después del Mundial, FIBA ha actualizado el ránking femenino de selecciones y, tras conseguir la medalla de bronce, España ha ascendido tres puestos para encaramarse a la tercera plaza. Por delante sólo tiene a Estados Unidos y Francia, los dos equipos que disputaron la final del campeonato. En su camino hacia el Top 3, la selección española ha superado a Australia, China y Bélgica, que le antecedían en la última clasificación. Ahora la posición de España parece sólida pues supera a Alemania, cuarta por más de 100 puntos mientras que está a unos 50 de la segunda posición de Francia. La tercera plaza es la mejor posición de España en el ránking FIBA femenino desde febrero de 2022, cuando llegó a estar segunda sólo por detrás de la inalcanzable Estados Unidos. Con la generación actual y las jóvenes que cada verano conquistan medallas en categorías de formación, viene una época esperanzadora para la selección femenina, que podría asentarle en ese Top 3 mundial.

articles.title: DeMar DeRozan's Reaction to Jokic, Gordon, Murray Recruiting Him to Nuggets and Kings Exit Revealed
articles.summary: Veteran guard DeMar DeRozan knows he's getting closer to the end of his career, but it means a lot that a perennial contender like the Denver Nuggets still wanted him following his departure from the Sacramento Kings.
articles.body:
Veteran guard DeMar DeRozan knows he's getting closer to the end of his career, but it means a lot that a perennial contender like the Denver Nuggets still wanted him following his departure from the Sacramento Kings.

While speaking to The Athletic's Mirin Fader , DeRozan revealed that Nuggets stars Nikola Jokić, Aaron Gordon and Jamal Murray all called him to recruit him to Denver, which influenced the 37-year-old's decision to sign with the team.

"When I came in the league, I never would have imagined or thought I'd be playing that long," DeRozan said. "And when you get in, you don't realize how fast and how much time goes by. … It's a blessing to be able to play this long."

Every NBA Team's Top Breakout Candidate This Upcoming Season 😀

2017 NBA Re-Draft Gives Teams the Ultimate Do-Overs 🏀

DeRozan spent the last two seasons with the Kings and was one of the few bright spots for a rebuilding team. He averaged 18.4 points, 2.9 rebounds and 4.1 assists during the 2025-26 season as Sacramento tied for the worst record in the Western Conference at 22-60. It was his first time averaging under 20 points since his fourth year in the league in 2012-13.

Despite the Kings' lack of success, DeRozan admitted that it was difficult to part ways with the franchise this offseason.

"You gain relationships with players, staff, people within the organization," DeRozan said. "It's always tough to leave. I was extremely close with a lot of people."
